records.our_prose: Dill is a light feeder and one of the few herbs that prefers lean soil; Utah State University notes that no additional nutrients are needed if the soil is amended at planting. Work a little compost in before sowing and, in poor ground, give one light feeding once the plants are growing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes dill lank and floppy and can dull the aromatic oils that give the leaves and seed their flavor. A plant grown on for seed or pickling heads needs no extra feeding once it bolts.

records.our_prose: In the maritime Pacific Northwest, dill gets a real break most of the country does not: our cool, mild summer rarely gets hot enough to bolt it the way a hot inland summer would. Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in late winter or early spring, since young dill takes a light frost, and sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady supply of leaves. Ease off new sowings around midsummer when the days are longest, then sow again in late summer for a fall crop that keeps going right up to the first frost. Dill self-sows readily, so volunteers often show up on their own the following spring.

records.source_context: However, be aware that vegetables planted in late summer or early fall (August or September) will be susceptible to insects and diseases that thrive in hot weather. Likewise, cold-tender vegetables planted in late winter or early spring may be damaged by frosts or freezes if not protected with covers (see "Extending the Gardening Season" above for more information on covers).

records.our_prose: Dill is not one of USU Extension's Table 1 vegetable rows, so this spring window follows the Group A (Hardy) February 15 date given to St. George's other cold-hardy spring crops. Leaves are ready in about 55 days from an April harvest; dill's own heat threshold runs around 78°F, so the plant bolts to seed heads and leaf quality drops once St. George's summer heat, which routinely reaches 100°F in June and July per USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation data, sets in. A second direct sowing in early August, once the worst heat has broken, follows USU's general fall-gardening guidance for restarting cool-season crops (Fall Gardening in the St. George Area); the fall stand crops from late September up to just ahead of the average November 1 first frost. Dill self-sows readily if a few heads are left standing.
